claims.text: Rapid synthesis of Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys induces metastable Mg-rich microsegregation.
Thermal exposure transforms metastable Mg-rich microsegregations into stable Mg-containing intermetallic compounds.
The resulting structural evolution promotes formation of a dense, protective Mg-oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation.
The structural evolution creates localized galvanic cells that alter aqueous corrosion behavior.
The initial non-equilibrium microstructure contains Mg-rich segregations.
The initial microstructure contains mixed solid-solution and incipient-intermetallic regions.
Controlled post-synthesis thermal aging can activate phase transformations.
Rapid solidification provides the non-equilibrium processing condition required by the proposed mechanism.
The investigated alloys are constrained to densities below 6 g/cm3.
Non-equilibrium processing creates local Mg enrichment at phase boundaries.
Mg-containing intermetallic compounds formed during aging preferentially oxidize.
Preferential oxidation of the transformed regions produces a coherent Mg-oxide layer at high temperature.
Chemical heterogeneity generated by phase transformation creates local galvanic differences in aqueous environments.
Local galvanic differences affect aqueous corrosion pathways.
After thermal aging, the rapidly processed alloy will have a more continuous Mg-oxide scale than it has in the as-synthesized state.
After thermal aging, the rapidly processed alloy will have a more protective Mg-oxide scale than it has in the as-synthesized state.
Thermal aging will alter corrosion behavior relative to both the initial state and near-equilibrium processed variants.
The altered corrosion behavior may include increased localized corrosion caused by galvanic cells.
Thermal-aging conditions can be chosen to activate phase transformation without causing complete homogenization.
